blocks.x: What's your name? My name? Your right name.
My name is Henry John Rutz.
Henry John Rutz, yes. And I'll put on here today, it's January the 18th, 1972, and we're just starting to talk to you. I wanted to ask you where you were born and when.
New Orleans, Louisiana. How do you mind doing today? 1903. August 7, 1903.
Was your family a musical?
My daddy and my uncle. Great.
What was their names?
Henry J. Rutz. My mother was Mary Rutz. And your uncle? My uncle, Bob Rutz. He was supposed to be the strongest charm on player in the city of New Orleans.
Who did they play with?

All of them. Monk Johnson. That's before my time. I was a baby. Yeah. I was a young baby then. I was a young baby. I saw my daddy play twice in my life. My uncle. My uncle and my dad were playing the same band. And I played with the old man Rube Show. Oh. I was a great man. I also played with Rube Show. Which I didn't know. And what else is there?
Well, I'm glad to know about that because you know I never knew much about your uncle or your father at all. I'm saying that.

They got lots of other little fellas and them. Not even in, y'all don't even have them. And the guys that give you the information, they got them, they don't have them anymore. Yeah. You got my point of view? Yeah, I agree with you.
I think it's a shame.

It don't sound right. If a guy wants to know about him and Russ Black, he says, well, I'm not. If I pass away, he'd be something else, you know. He's a younger fella than me, twenty-five years younger than me. And he'd tell them, say, well, how about Henry Russ? Well, Henry Russ used to do so and so and so and so. See? But he'd say, well, I don't know all his life, but you can find him at such a place.
You get my point? Oh, absolutely. You're the one who knows the most about it.
I'm saying that, but they come up and give you information about me and they know you know me.
Yeah.

But I did play with me, you know, recently, you see. But they don't know my life. They're twenty-five years younger than me. They don't know when I started. They don't know all the bands I played with. You know what I mean? But they would be in the rocks.
Do you remember Bonk, by the way?
No, I remember Bonk. That's when my daddy used to do it.
Yeah, but you remember him at that time?
Not at that time. My daddy was playing with him. I was a kid.
You were too little.
I was a monk at Packley, quit playing. When I started out in music, I mean when I got families. How old were you when you started playing? I was nineteen years old.
What was your first instrument? What was your first instrument?
I started out on drums.
Did you take lessons from anybody?
I took lessons from Louis Dumas. You got him in the book. We had him. Yeah. He'd have a certain part of him.
And then you started taking lessons when you were nineteen? No. Or you started just when you started playing professors?
I started taking lessons when I was a fan about five or six years.
And then when you turned nineteen you started playing professors?
Well, you take at least five or six years to get professors.
Yeah, I understand.

And see, the average musician there, he goes out for what they got to do. He don't go out for big time. See, when I started, I was going out for the biggest band in the city. Maybe go to New York. Luke Elton, I had the opportunity to go there a couple of times. See, but I was making much money here that they were making in New York. And I had my family.
What was the first band you stayed with?
Tillman. Oh, yeah?
That's right.
That's right. He and I raised up together. Are you from uptown? I'm from Sixteen Ward. Is that Carrollton?
That's Carrollton.
Tillman's from up there. That's very recent. He's four years old anymore.
Well, when you were a kid, did you fool around with any little homemade instruments or anything like that, like Tillman did?
He fooled. Tillman played fool with the clarinet.
Oh, I thought he fooled around with a tin flute and stuff like that.
No. Oh, we were. Yeah, we were. We were fooling around with a flute, you know. Yeah? The bomb fifteen cents flute at the dragon stone.
Oh, I see.
Yeah, that was our philosophy, you know. And, uh, well, Tillman and I raised up together. His brother-in-law, you got Alan Gorda in there?
Mm-hmm.
Well, that's his brother-in-law.
Yeah, I met his brother.
We all started out together. Mm-hmm. We all raised up together.
Mm-hmm.

Tillman, call him Hunter, we can call him Hunter, his name is Alan Gorda. Mm-hmm. Willie Newton, Joe Mudhouse, Old Man Nighy, well Tillman's brother, he started playing, but he didn't last long, he didn't stay too long. That was the band that was the first band we started up.
And Tillman was playing clarinet then? Correct. And you were playing drums? I was playing drums. Where did Willie Newton play? The bass of all of them. Well, who is Liberty Newton?
Liberty Newton. Did you ever hear of him?
No.
I don't know who else. I don't know, that's the only one I know is Willie Newton. Yeah, well. I never heard of another Willie Newton at all.
Somebody might have gotten the name mixed up too. Probably so, yeah. But you knew him well, so you know him.
Oh, we played together a long time.
And who was playing trumpet in the band? Gordak.
Gordak, yeah, yeah.
And, what was the guy's name, Mud, uh? Mudhouse was playing bandit.
He was a much older man than us. Mudhouse. Yeah, he called him Joe Mudhouse.
Yeah, that wasn't his right name?

Well, his name was Joe now. Yeah. But I'm not thinking, I'm thinking this is Joe. Joe's about thinking still, man. He's got a son living today. Oh. But he was, oh, he was, he was in my dad's class. He played around my dad that time. He was one of the one that picked us up, you know, and get a little, a few jobs, and we go on with him, we get jobs, and we check him with us, I think.
You know how old your daddy was when you were born?
How old he was? Yeah. Well, my daddy was 72 when he died. And what year did he die? The 51. 51. So, yeah, he was, Joe Mudhouse was way ahead of you.
He was here 20 years at the back. Oh, yeah. Much.
Yeah. Much 20 years now.
We see, we got drums, and we got bass and trumpet, and you played trombone? A saxophone?
That was Chairman's brother. Oh, yeah. He started to play in trombone. But he didn't, he didn't, he didn't stay with us, you know.
What was that, Eddie? Edward.
Edward, yeah. He didn't play, oh, he didn't play. I don't think he played six or eight months. Then he cut out of me. But he got in bed coming, and he cut out.
Well, he never did look healthy, didn't he?

Hmm? He never did look too healthy. Well, he was a young man at that time. Yeah. Now, me and Edward was back the same age, you know. Edward might be a year old with me, or maybe I might be the same age. But Tim was two years old, three years old at me. Hmm. Well, where did you play with this band? All over the city. Used to play all over. Used to feature, used to feature me at all times.
Mm-hmm.
Yes, I was playing during my, I used to sing. Takes so long for them, gentlemen. They'd feature me as Kid Nats. You know who they're talking about? Kid which? Kid Nats. No.
Kid Nats.
Never heard of that.
Did you see? Yeah.
It's in the book, you got to listen to John. Yeah. He got my name in there, Henry Russ, Kid Nats Shaker. Yeah.
I mean, I got a gang of them.

I remember Shaker. Well, I got Kid Nats in there too. Why'd they call you Shaker? Yeah, just a worried guy would call me, you know. Just a worried man, now, H. You know H. You know H. You know H. You know H. You give me that man.
He's always doing that.

Well, H. You know H. He's not always me, but he's not too far behind me. Yeah. And we were playing the same band, and we were playing Captain Handley, you know. And he started to call me Shaker. That's my new drum man. His first band you played with Jim and Jim, how long did that band play with him? Well, that band did get us all out of the band. I mean, you have to elevate yourself, see.
Yeah.

How long did you play with Jim and Jim? Oh, it must have been about two, three years. And after all, the other band, they had a gang of bands around there, a small band. They had no big band around those. No 12, 13-piece bands. The biggest band he had around there was six, seven pieces.
So what band did you do in the African band?
I done Foster Lewis band. Foster Lewis band. Excuse me, yeah. Foster Lewis band.
Who was in that band?

I knew him, Foster Lewis. Jude Foster. We had nicknames, but the real name is Foster. That word's name is Lewis Foster. We called him Foster Lewis. He did a great German one band. Jude Foster was his brother. Trumpet.
Yeah, I knew him.
Leo Sanjee. We don't even have him in the book.
He was a band-joke band? That's right. Yeah, I know about him.

Somebody gave you a story about me. I didn't give you the right thing. He the one that got me in the band. got me in the band. Joe Phillip Jr., he's calling One-Eyed Bass. Oh, the old man on bass. That one. Correct. Joe Phillip. Joe Phillip Jr., he was starting out. You mean Gatun was starting out? Yeah, I see. The son. Yeah. He was starting out. And he had a boy, a pretty kind of Henry. Henry, Henry. They were on Gemma Street there.
Did he live near this guy Franklin? Huh? Did he live near this guy Franklin? What? Did he live near this guy named

Franklin? They called him Dog? Henry Franklin. Oh, that's the same guy? That's the same guy. That's the same guy. That was the Clownest player. But I played with that band. We had a friend of mine, a guy that started me out to a friend. I didn't have no instrument at all. Let me turn it off. Yeah, go ahead. So, we had a friend of mine, a friend of mine, all of us, I mean, Willie Leboeuf. That's his real man. He's called him Wooligan. Oh, yeah. And he's the one. During them days, most all the drummers had three-four sets of drums. Had them, it was broke, it was thrown on the side, and by a new one. I didn't even have a drum. Yeah, I used to play it from a wooden wall. I wanted a tub. And he and I was a good friend. I mean, he was a much older man than I was. But we sprung together, drink together. I was nothing but a kid. He was a gone man. I mean, he went to a little. He made a set of drums for me to go play with Foster Lewis. Finally, we played, after I left Tillman. Garnup, called myself Garnup, and Foster Lewis had a pretty good band. He was like, he was just, I mean, I just spent a year, it's all gone good. Oh shit. David Foster Lewis, who, um.
Was that a reading band, or? Huh? Was that a reading band or a fake band?

Oh, they could, they could spell, but they're. But they didn't use a ring? No, they didn't. Tillman didn't need it, huh? Wasn't using that much music, you know. Did Tillman use any music in your band? Well, he could spell too, but he didn't use it. Otherwise, this was a fake band. Yeah, mostly faking, you know. A lot of guys say, playing by hearing. Yeah. But you're in such a thing, playing by hearing. You're faking.

That's what you call faking. See? Oh. I forgot to ask you, when, when Lewis Dumaine gave, gave you lessons, did he teach you reading, or you're playing drum? He taught me reading. Uh-huh. That's right. Drum music, that's right. I was, that's right, yeah. He didn't teach any other instruments?
Yeah, he taught me trumpet too. Oh, he did? Yeah. Uh.
What about the bass? Did you take lessons from that too, or you're six at a minute? I know all that.
I took lessons. I took lessons. I took lessons. I took lessons. I took lessons. I took lessons. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. All I, I knew the music, but all I'd do was study the bass when I, it's all the
playing bass, father. Uh-huh. So Dumaine taught you both trumpet and drums?

Uh-huh. Yeah. He taught me both trumpet and drums. Uh-huh. Lewis Dumaine and George McCullum. I see. You heard the talking. Yeah. Uh-huh. Well, I went on from there, and when I was playing about, just about four years, I thought of playing with Lewis Dumaine. Lewis Dumaine said, well, don't you learn how to read? He was very strict, you know. He was mostly, that's the most he could play. About music, he couldn't play, couldn't play, you know. But I, I, the other guy said, man, you learn how to read, man, you're not going to be able to play nothing. But I, I went along with it, you know. Uh-huh. So, I said, well, I mean, I'm going to stick my mind and make up my mind and start learning how to read. Not for no particular reason, see. Well, after I got to study music, he learned me how to play drum, he gave me the idea of drum music, division, give me division. Well, I played with this band a while. See, I care what I was playing with. And I continued reading, about, about two, three methods. And I played on with him. Then I go to another band. After the work got slow, I go to the Louisiana, New Jersey, you know who I'm talking about, Willie Connich. Played with that band about two years.
Who was in that band? Huh?

Do you remember who he was in that band? Yeah. There's one boy. I know his first name, but I can't, I don't know, I forgot his name. Willie Connich, myself, Charlie Toad, Miss Toad, his wife, and his brother.
His brother played band there? Correct, yeah.

And Charlie played, uh, bass ball. And the wife? And his wife played piano. That's right. And this boy, Ulyss, forget his last name. I know he's doing the name. What instrument was that? Trumpet. Ulyss, yeah. What's the trumpet play?
Oh, he used to play with Joey Lewis at one time. Joey Lewis? Yeah, I think about 45. I don't know. Somebody. Is he from downtown? A real bright guy?
He's from down here. He's from down here.
He lived in Baton Rouge, I think. I don't know. I haven't seen him. He's got a brother named Nelson? Is that the one?

No, no. No. I haven't seen that boy in years. He got out to Middick World for some reason. He got out to Middick World. And, uh, I played with that band quite a while. So, after I left that band, I go to the Supreme Band. And then, that's Eddie Jackson, Peter Lacasse, Phil, Colbeck, Nick Nairn. Uh, we weren't even in the piano that much. I think old man Humphrey, not William Humphrey, his daddy.
What did he call him?
Clown at, side of the phone.
Yeah, yeah, another one.
And after, I left that band.
How wrong with you was then? Huh? How wrong with you was then?
I was about 1925, 26. Uh-huh. Yeah.
Did he say,
Curbeck? What did he play?
Curbeck. He's pretty sacrifice. We left here a year. Curbeck. He called him Curbeck.
Oh, Curbeck. Yeah.
Pill. Yeah. The people who were.
Cripple Pill. Yeah.
Who was the leader of the band?
Oh, Pee LaCasse. Oh, Pee LaCasse. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Eddie Jackson was the manager.
Uh-huh.
And I stayed away from that band in about two years.
And what did they call the band, you said?
The Supreme.
Oh, yeah.

The Supreme Band. They was a band in about two years or two and a half years. I joined, I rejoined in Louisiana, jazz town again. I was playing at the Royal Garden on Graber Street. Must have been around about twenty-six. Stay with that band two years. The people of Cass and them come back and they heard me play with the Blue-Kanami jazz town at the Royal Garden. And I hadn't seen them, they hadn't seen me. And they come up there and say, don't I know you?
I said, maybe you do.
You know your name Henry Rush? I said, yeah. Well, at that time, the Supreme Band had broke up completely. So they renamed the band as the Nolan.
So that's more or less the same band, then?
It's more or less the same band, but they renamed the band. But Eddie Jackson got out the band. I see. They put Eddie Jackson out the band.
And then, who did they have at that time?
Oh, they got a boy. I don't forget this boy in there.
What is he?
Space violence. Eddie Jackson was the manager.
Uh-huh.
Pete LeCasse was the leader.
But the Nolan band, then Eddie Jackson was out.
Yeah, he was completely out.
Yeah. And whose band was it then?
Pete LeCasse band.
Uh-huh.
Yeah. Pete LeCasse took the band over.
Do you remember anybody else in that band? Yeah.
Pete LeCasse. Uh-huh. Let me see who was French. Arthur William Clannett. Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. He had a whole trumpet.
He wasn't using the piano at that time.
A trumpet.
Pete LeCasse.
Oh, I see. Only one?
One trumpet at that time. They never did have started using two trumpets, yeah? Yeah. Around 1930. 1929 and 30. See, around 1929 or 30. They stopped using. They stopped in large and big.
That was just a small-sized band, about six feet.
That's all they had during them days. During them days.
Did you ever know a guy named Durium?
Durium.
Durium. Something like that. Who's a trombone player.
Durium. I can't recall, but maybe I did.
What about Booker Washington? Did you ever know him?
I never knew him. We played in the last band together. That's the band, that's the guy you see in the Navy band. That's the bass player. Frank Fever's playing ghetto. He was the bass player.
Who played the Clannett in the Nola band? Who did you say, what's that, Arthur Williams?
Arthur Williams, yeah.
He didn't use the Pico in the Nola band?
No, we wasn't using no saxophone. Until later on, we used saxophone. Years later, we started being lost in the band.
What year did the Nola band start? What year was it named the Nola band, do you think? In the late 20s, sometime?
Late 20s, yeah. About 20. I was about 26, 27.
Before the Depression hit, in other words.
Yeah. What time did it? Just before. I thought, left the Louisiana Jazz on, I go to the Nola band.
And he said that you didn't use no piano. Did he else have to band you?
During that time, he wasn't using no piano, because they didn't have no piano at the place where we were playing at.
Where were you playing at?
Yeah. At the Royal Garden.
Uh-huh.
On gravel between Padilla and Jazz. And I go to the Nola band. In 1925, I think, or 26, the Pelican opened. The Pelican opened. Well, we go to the Pelican.
With the Nola band? Yes.
With the Nola band. With the baby, originally was a house band.
Uh-huh.

That was where his brother was on the place. Now, in the rhythm. He was. Oh. And we go to the Pelican. We played the Pelican about three, four years. Uh-huh. See? And I played on the Pelican. Depression was coming in. I come in all the time. I played in the Nola band until about. He said, I didn't know the band. I don't know. I don't want to play. And the Nola band was changed to the Silverton officer. That's the time old man Duce had taken the band over. Old man Duce. Not Sam Duce, but his daddy.
The Clarence play.
His daddy.
Was Pete Lacat still in the band then?
That was the band, Sam Banner. They said, he took the band over. He just changed the name.
I see.
From the Nola to the Silverton.
And then they got rid of the other Clarence play. Huh? They got rid of Arthur?
No.
He stayed in the band?
The old man Duce was playing saxophone.
Oh, I see.
He was playing Clarence.
I see.
Yeah. This boy just died there a couple of months ago, a couple of years ago. He was saxophone playing. That's when he started increasing the band, when the Pelican opened up.
He started using piano too?
Well, we had piano up there. We started using piano. We'd use piano while they had or nothing. It didn't happen when they couldn't use them. Yeah.
Who played piano?
Well, we had a lady piano played most of the time. Miss Camilla Todd. That's just the other girl, man. That's what I mean. Camilla Todd. Willie Mina.
Oh, he won't be in the ball.
That's good. Never born. She died too, I heard. Never born. Jewelry Street. I can't call her any of them.
The lady who used to play with Solistan about 49? Oh, Miss Kimball came here?
You told me Miss Kimball. No, no. She used to play with all the bands. Yeah. I'm trying to call them in.
Well, there's Olivia Charlotte or Mercedes Gormand.
Mercedes Gormand.
Yeah.
Mercedes Gormand. Yeah. When you—I thought we had most of the time was women's piano players. We had one or two men's piano players around there.
Did you start using two trumpets to that also?
Well, during that time, yeah.
Who did you have a trumpet?

Well, during that time we were going to Perrikan. We would use Son Allen. He'd look at—we had to have a big band up there. He's playing mostly—we had two bands, you see? One band in each corner. Baby Every Wizzley band, maybe Outer Town band, you know? Clayborne Williams band. We used two bands. We used to play a band. We used to play a band. And we'd use two trumpets. Son Allen, we'd get this boy Shots, a record.
You changed your own a little bit.
Huh?
Your personality changed a little bit.
Well, the guy played a band a certain while and he could promote it. He'd do it in another band. He wouldn't make the most money.
What did Peter Lokos play like then?
Trumpets.
Oh, but I mean, what kind? Would he be playing first? Would he be playing greatly?
He was a strictly first man. Was he—
Strictly. Did he get off at all? He was no solo man.
He got off to his own— He was a first chair man.
I see.
You couldn't find a better chair man. You like George McCullum?
Mm-hmm.
He wasn't no hot man, but you couldn't find a— And what you want, your chair man is first.
Oh, yeah. Mm-hmm.
Chair man is first. When you got to have— But you got to have a— You got to have a feature man on the side.
When you got to have that bigger band, then you started using music, I guess, too, huh?
Well, during that time, yeah, we was going up to music.
You had to use music with the band.
Yeah, when I left— I left— When I left for them small bands, and I went to an older band, I had to read music.
Where did you get the music?
Yeah?
Where did they get the music?
They brought it from the music store.
They wasn't— They wouldn't get any specials then. Yeah? They didn't have any special arrangements, huh?
Well, not very few, no. We didn't have any special arrangements.
He asked for the stocks.
Yeah, we— They moved to stocks.
You didn't have any arrangements in the band?
Mm-mm. No. I never have known any arrangements. I used to write a re-copy, you know? Mm-hmm. We'd go to the music store and buy a pianoscopy.
Mm-hmm.
And it wasn't much of a song. The people asked for them, well, they'd give me the pianoscopy, and I'd go and I'd re-copy and transport it.
Right out of stocks for them.
Mm-hmm. So, after I left that band, I played in that band until depression got great.
Listen, I think I thought of some people's names I wanted to ask you about. Uh-huh. And we can come back just to leave it in the middle of that.
Yeah, yeah.
Did you ever know a saxophone player named T-Boy? T-Boy?

Yeah. That's—that's—now that's—that's one mistake they made in my life. Mm-hmm. That's why I'm asking you. I mean—yeah, yeah, yeah. Excuse me. Why I had that flu, man. Uh, T-Boy was a trumpet player. Mm-hmm.
Oh, huh?
He was a trumpet player. Yeah.
You don't remember his last name?
Huh?
You don't remember his last name?
T-Boy, what do I mean?
Oh, yeah. That's who I thought it might be, you know.
That's why— Yeah, I know. He was a trumpet player.
Did you play with him?
Yeah.
What band?
Oh, I think he was playing with Chris Kelly.
Oh.

No, no. Chris Kelly was a trumpet player. T-Boy, when he carried his band, he carried his band four at the time. His own band? Yeah. He carried his band. And, uh, he had a bass player. Another T-Boy, but he's—he's another T-Boy. Oh, I—he's his last name.
Well, the one that I know about that played bass used to play with Little Dad.
Correct.
Yeah, is that the same guy?
That's right.
Eddie Gilmore.
That's right. A little short, but he had—he had a full—he had a full-size bass. We used to laugh at him when he took his bass down.
But who was the bass player with the Nola band?
Uh, I'm trying to call this—we had a boy by the name of R.T. That's a— R.T. That's all right. R.T., yeah.
That's a—I was fine. I was fine.

And, uh, they used to call him R.T. And, uh, another guy used to play with the Nola band. Was playing with the Nola band when I went to Nola band after Eddie Jassie. I can't think of that boy named, uh, to save my life. He was a pretty good—he was Gene Bush bass player, too. I'm trying to call this man. I can't call it. Well, don't worry about it. We'll think of it. It'll come, then. Yeah, can I? Maybe. Yeah. I'll think about it.
Did you know a trumpet player named John—uh, Ulyss John?

Ulyss John. Yeah. That's the boy I'm trying to call his name. That's the one you were thinking about a while ago? That's the one I'm trying to call his name. From Boundtown. Oh, I see. That's the one. Ulyss John is his name. That's the boy. Yeah. I knew his name was Ulyss, but I didn't know his—I forgot his last name. Yeah. And, uh, going back to the Nola band, huh?
Yeah, yeah. I just wanted to check back.
And I—yeah, that's the boy I'm in. Ulyss John.
Yeah. Yeah.

So I played with the Silitone office, you know, I was dancing from the Nola band to the Silitone office. Uh-huh. And I played the Silitone office for about six, seven years. About five or six years. And I—not the Silitone, I mean including the whole entire band. Yeah. There was a depression set in. T-Rone was practically the biggest band in the city. And while I was playing on the Pelican, you know it was the Silitone band, Fred Marble was on the board. He came—he came up there, tried to get me to go on the board with him. Uh, at that time, the boat was all right, but I didn't care about traveling, gee. But he used to be there again, go up the line, gee. And I had my family. And I wanted to stay close to my family. Very little traveling at that time. Well, I come to fit Marble Down. So I stayed around there. After a while, I leave the—the Silitone office. I go to A.G. A.G. So I go to the A.G. A.P. room. And I played with the band about two years. So maybe a little less, couldn't be too much less. I was playing with the move card. Well, he had the great—he had—he was one of the greatest, one of the greatest in the city.
Remember who was in the band? Huh? Remember who was in that band?
Yeah, I'm going to call that man. One of the greatest piano players. Neil Peel.
Pio,
A.J. Piron, Marcel, Peter Boca,
P. Trompet? Yeah.
That is the other name again. Henry Boca. Henry Boca.
No, no, no, no, no, no.
Eddie Pearson.
No. This is from the 30s. This is from the 30s.
Yeah, early 30s. Eddie Pearson. He'll...
Yeah, Henry Boca was playing something. Not Henry, he's baseball.
Pete Boca was playing something.
Yeah. Henry was in the band.
He was playing bass. Oh, he was playing...
Sucephone. Sucephone. Yeah.
No, sucephone. He was telling me to use the bass drum, which he didn't use in bass drum. And I was... He was a little boy in there. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Was he before or after Lily Warner?
Lily Warner was going back.
Oh, Lily Warner was going back. He kept on getting in a long time, didn't he?
Oh, he had to be the Pope of the town, man. He's playing all of Richard's jobs in the city.
I guess that's how he kept the same man. Huh?
Yeah, he was going, he was the best band in the city. I mean, Marvin, I mean, his band is his type, you know, during them years.
